parts.title: Learning to swim at thirty
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Until last year, I could not swim. When I was a child, I fell into a river, and after that, I was always afraid of deep water. At thirty, I decided that enough was enough, and I joined a beginners' class at my local pool.

The first lesson was terrifying. I stood in the shallow end, holding the side, while eight children ran past me. My teacher, a patient woman called Rosa, did not laugh. She told me to put my face in the water for just three seconds, and I managed it.

Week by week, I got braver. By week four, I could float on my back, and by week six, I swam a whole length. I felt so proud that I nearly cried. Rosa took a photo of me at the end of the pool, and I still have it on my fridge.

Now I swim twice a week before work. It is the best way to clear my head. Last month, I even swam in the sea on holiday. My friends could not believe it.

options: She fell in a river once
questions.explanation: She says she fell into a river as a child.

questions.explanation: She calls the first lesson terrifying.

options: Put her face in the water
questions.explanation: She told her to put her face in the water for three seconds.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel in week six?
questions.explanation: She felt so proud that she nearly cried.

questions.explanation: She swims twice a week before work.

parts.title: How swimming became a sport
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
People have swum for thousands of years, but swimming did not become a sport until the nineteenth century. [1] In 1837, London held the first swimming competitions, which used a slow, simple style.

Then a new style arrived from South America. [2] It was faster, and soon everybody wanted to learn it.

In 1896, swimming was part of the first modern Olympic Games. [3] The swimmers raced in the open sea, and the water was so cold that some of them nearly gave up.

Swimming pools became common in the twentieth century. [4] They allowed people to train all year, even when the weather was bad.

Today, children all over the world learn to swim at school. [5] It is one of the few sports that people can enjoy from childhood until old age.
sentences: Indoor pools were built in most towns.
Fish can swim much faster than any human.
Before that, most people swam only to stay clean or to find food.
Many countries teach it in primary school because it can save lives.
People called it the crawl, and it looked very different from the old style.
There were only a few races, and all the competitors were men.

gaps.explanation: Before the nineteenth century people swam for other reasons; the next sentence gives the first competitions.
The new style was called the crawl; the next sentence says it was faster.
There were few races at the first Olympics; the next sentence says the swimmers raced in the open sea.
Indoor pools were built in towns, and the next sentence says they allowed training all year.
Schools teach swimming because it saves lives; the next sentence says it is a sport for all ages.

parts.title: Staying safe in the water
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Every summer, many accidents happen in the water, [1] you should always follow some simple rules. Never swim alone, and never swim [2] you have eaten a big meal. Check where the lifeguard is [3] you get into the water. If you swim in a river or the sea, remember that currents can be strong. If you are caught in one, do not try to swim against it. Instead, swim sideways [4] you are free. Children should always be watched by an adult, even if they [5] swim well. Finally, wear sunscreen and drink water, because it is easy to forget how hot it is when you are [6] the water.

gaps.explanation: So gives the result: accidents happen, so you should follow rules.
Never swim after you have eaten a big meal.
Check the lifeguard before you get into the water.
Swim sideways until you are free of the current.
Even if they can swim well: ability.
In the water means inside the water.

parts.title: A welcome at the Riverside Pool
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: manager
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to the Riverside Swimming Pool. My name is Gil, and I am the manager. We open at seven in the morning and close at nine in the evening, except on Sundays, when we close at six. Today, I want to tell you about our new classes. The beginners' course takes place on Wednesdays, and it costs thirty-five pounds for six weeks. If you want to improve your technique, you can join the advanced course on Fridays. For children, we have a special class on Saturday mornings, with games and music. All classes are taught by qualified teachers, and the maximum number in each group is eight. To book, you can call us or visit the reception desk. Remember that everyone must take a shower before entering the water. Thank you for listening.

parts.title: An interview with a champion swimmer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Sidra, you won a national swimming title at eighteen. When did you start swimming?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: At four, because my mother was worried about me near water. I loved it immediately, and by seven I was swimming for a club.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is a typical training day?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I get up at five, swim for two hours, go to school, and swim again in the evening. On Sundays, I rest completely.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is it ever boring?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Honestly, sometimes. You look at a black line on the bottom of the pool for hours. I plan what to eat afterwards.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you eat?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A lot of pasta, rice and fruit. I eat six times a day, because swimming uses a great deal of energy.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What was your proudest moment?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Winning the title, of course, but also helping a younger swimmer who was crying before a race. She came second, and she hugged me.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What are your plans?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I would like to qualify for the Olympics, but first I have to finish my exams.
